label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: Two-week Arctic outbreak across the Northeast. NYCA winter peak load runs 10% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.10) and Henry Hub rises 40% (gas_hh_pct 40). Upstate WEST has surplus supply, but the transfer paths into Zone J are saturated and downstate oil and gas units are scarce. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $140/MWh on every one of the 14 shocked days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 140). The spread widening hits the P5 retail obligation hardest, because its loss also scales with load. The P2 long spread (+$1.5M) and the P1/P4 long WEST gains (+$0.4M, from higher load and gas) only partly offset it. I added no extra WEST move, DART shock or price spike, so the loss comes purely from the zone-volume and congestion channel. The estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities (about $3.9k per $/MWh per day net for P2 plus P5, which assumes the effect is linear in duration) and is uncertain.

Prolonged 20-day winter cold with gas-constrained downstate. Henry Hub rises 80% (gas_hh_pct 80) and NYCA peak load runs 12% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.12). A constrained export path leaves WEST on-peak 35% softer than the gas and load shocks imply (ref_onpeak_pct -35), because upstate hydro, nuclear and wind cannot reach the load pocket. This cuts the P1 swap and P4 heat-rate call payoffs. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $80/MWh for the full duration (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80), which hurts P5 and is only partly offset by P2. The higher load enlarges the P5 obligation. The P1/P4 gains from higher gas and load are largely cancelled by the negative WEST residual. I set the New York gas basis and DART shocks to zero. The loss estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities assuming linearity, and shocks do not add exactly, so it is uncertain.

Short, severe 8-day cold event with a very strong N.Y.C. premium. Load is 15% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.15, inside the historical maximum of 1.196). Henry Hub rises 30% (gas_hh_pct 30) and New York gas basis adds $15/MMBtu to the P4 gas cost (ny_gas_basis_usd 15). That basis shock lowers P4 only; it does not move power prices. WEST on-peak is 25% below what the gas and load shocks imply (ref_onpeak_pct -25), since the stress is concentrated downstate. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $220/MWh on each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 220), well inside the historical maximum of 400. The P5 retail load loss grows with both the wide spread and the high load, and dominates the P2 gain and the small P1 and P4 changes. The estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, so it is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long winter cold regime with a persistent but moderate downstate squeeze. NYCA peak load runs 10% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.10) and Henry Hub is 30% higher (gas_hh_pct 30). Transfers into Zone J stay constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $60/MWh wider on every day of the 30-day duration (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60). This is a smaller daily shock than my earlier runs but lasts the whole horizon, which keeps it closer to historical spread levels. WEST on-peak is 15% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -15), as upstate surplus generation is stranded. That trims the P1 and P4 gains and also weakens the WEST leg of the P5 hedge. P5 loses heavily because the obligation scales with load. P2 recovers part of this. There is no DART shock or price spike. The loss is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities assuming linearity, so it is uncertain.

A 25-day cold period in which forecasts keep under-predicting load, so real-time clears above day-ahead. Real-time prices are 150% above day-ahead (dart_pct 150), which hurts the P3 receiver of day-ahead minus real-time, though only slightly. Load runs 12% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.12) and Henry Hub is 60% higher (gas_hh_pct 60). Congestion into N.Y.C. is heavy, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $90/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 90) for all 25 days. That is the main loss, through the load-scaled P5 obligation. WEST on-peak is 30% below the gas-and-load implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -30), which mutes the P1 and P4 gains and the WEST hedge leg of P5. P2 offsets some of the loss. This scenario combines the DART channel with a long squeeze. The loss is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, assuming linearity, so it is uncertain.

A 12-day high-load cold event with a fuel-cost squeeze. Load is 15% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.15), within the historical maximum, and Henry Hub rises 40% (gas_hh_pct 40). A New York gas basis of $5/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 5) raises the gas cost in the P4 heat-rate call only, so it erodes P4 without moving power prices. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $140/MWh on each of the 12 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 140), which is below the historical maximum of 400. WEST on-peak is 25% softer than the gas and load shocks imply (ref_onpeak_pct -25), so the P1 gain is cut and the WEST hedge leg of P5 loses value. The P5 loss is large because the high load multiplies the wide spread. P2 offsets part of it. The loss is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities, assuming linearity, so it is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A 12-day summer heat wave lifts the daily peak load to 1.15 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.15). Transfers from upstate into N.Y.C. are constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $160/MWh on every shocked day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 160, below the historical maximum of 289.7). This hurts P5, the N.Y.C. retail load obligation, which is short N.Y.C. against only a WEST hedge, and its loss grows with load. P2 gains only about one fifth of what P5 loses. The higher load adds small gains on the long WEST positions P1 and P4. Gas, real-time/day-ahead, WEST on-peak and spike shocks are all set to zero so the loss comes purely from the zone-volume and congestion channel. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities (P5 about -20.9k and P2 about +3.8k per $1 of widening per 5 days) to 12 days. Net loss is roughly $7M. That is an extrapolation, not an engine result.

A short, intense 6-day summer heat wave pushes peak load to 1.3 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.3). N.Y.C. real-time scarcity pricing opens a very wide locational gap, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 250, inside the historical maximum of 289.7). The June 2025 heat event is a loose analogue: N.Y.C. real-time on-peak was about $625.5 against about $416.5 in WEST. The loss falls on P5, which is short N.Y.C. with only a WEST hedge and has its volume scaled up by high load. P2 offsets about one fifth of the P5 loss, and the extra load gives small gains on P1 and P4. All other shocks are zero, so the loss is isolated to congestion and zone volume at higher intensity but shorter duration than S1. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities to 6 days with a 1.3 load multiplier on P5. It gives a net loss of about $6.5M with real uncertainty, because the spread response may not be linear.

A prolonged 25-day hot summer spell keeps load 12% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.12). The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread stays $75/MWh wider throughout (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75), as a persistent transmission and generation squeeze in the N.Y.C. pocket. The small shock repeated over many days grinds down P5, the N.Y.C. load obligation, and its loss is amplified by the higher load. P2 offsets about one fifth of it. A $3/MMBtu gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) applies to the heat-rate call P4 only and trims its payoff slightly. WEST prices and Henry Hub are left unshocked because a rise there would help the long positions. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities fivefold and nets small gains from load. Net loss is roughly $6.3M. This is an extrapolation, so confidence is low.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 20-day summer heat wave lifts peak load to 1.10 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.10). Upstate generation is bottled behind transmission limits while N.Y.C. is short. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $80/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80, well inside the historical maximum of 289.7), and the WEST on-peak price falls a further 30% (ref_onpeak_pct -30) because surplus upstate energy cannot reach the city. The widening spread is what hurts P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation, whose loss grows with load. The lower WEST price takes away the gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, which would otherwise offset part of the loss. P2 gains about one fifth of the P5 loss. Gas, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The estimate scales the supplied 5-day sensitivities (P5 about -3,950 per $/MWh-day, P2 about +650) and nets the P1/P4 effects. It is an extrapolation, not an engine result.

A hot summer month (30 days, the full horizon) leaves the daily peak load at a typical-day level (load_peak_ratio 1.0, the minimum allowed for a heat wave). Persistent N.Y.C. transfer limits keep the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread $60/MWh wider on every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60, far below the historical maximum of 289.7). That is a small shock repeated over many days, which keeps the scenario close to historical conditions. The loss comes almost entirely from P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation short N.Y.C. against only a WEST hedge. P2 returns about 16% of the P5 loss. Because load is not raised, P1 and P4 collect no load-driven gains. All other shocks are zero. The estimate scales the supplied sensitivities, with P5 at about -3,950 per $/MWh-day and P2 at about +650 over 1,800 $/MWh-days. It is an extrapolation.

A 30-day hot summer with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Day-ahead over-schedules the heat, so real-time clears 20% below day-ahead (dart_pct -20). Upstate WEST on-peak prices are a further 20% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -20) from mild upstate weather and ample supply. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $45/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45) as the city stays tight. P5 is the main loser, short N.Y.C. with a WEST hedge. Lower WEST prices cut the gains on the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 below the unshocked path. The short real-time/day-ahead position P3 gains slightly, and P2 offsets part of the P5 loss. Gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate adds the scaled 5-day sensitivities (P5 and P2 from the spread, P1 and P4 from the price cuts) and assumes they are roughly additive. Real uncertainty remains on that assumption.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day hot summer with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Surplus upstate generation depresses the WEST on-peak price a further 40% (ref_onpeak_pct -40). That removes the price gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. N.Y.C. stays tight, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $50/MWh wider every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50, far inside the 289.7 historical maximum). The widening spread is the main loss, falling on P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation short N.Y.C. with only a WEST hedge. P2 returns about 18% of it. Gas, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The estimate scales the observed spread results (P5 about -3.4k and P2 about +0.6k per $/MWh-day) and the supplied price sensitivities for P1 and P4. It is an extrapolation, not an engine result.

A 30-day hot summer with slightly elevated peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.05). Day-ahead over-procures for the heat, so real-time clears 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40). This lowers the realized WEST prices on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and gives only a small gain on P3. The WEST on-peak price is a further 30% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -30) from ample upstate supply. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $45/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45) as the city stays constrained. The spread and the extra load drive the loss on P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation, and P2 offsets only part of it. Gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate adds the scaled sensitivities and assumes they are roughly additive, so it is uncertain, and P4 may lose less than I assume.

An 18-day summer heat spell at typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Transfer limits into N.Y.C. widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $100/MWh on each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 100, inside the 289.7 historical maximum). This is the main loss, on P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation short N.Y.C. against only a WEST hedge, with P2 offsetting about 18%. WEST on-peak is a further 35% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -35) because upstate energy is bottled, which removes the gains on P1 and P4. A $3/MMBtu N.Y. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) applies to the heat-rate call P4 only, and further lowers its payoff. Henry Hub, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The estimate scales the observed spread results (P5 about -3.4k per $/MWh-day, P2 about +0.6k) and nets the P1 and P4 price effects. It is an extrapolation.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer heat period with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Upstate supply is abundant and the WEST on-peak price falls a further 50% (ref_onpeak_pct -50), so the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 lose their price gains. N.Y.C. stays tight, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $40/MWh wider every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 40, far below the 289.7 historical maximum). That hurts P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation short N.Y.C. with only a WEST hedge, and P2 offsets about 18% of the loss. A $4/MMBtu N.Y. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 4) applies to P4 only and cuts its payoff. Henry Hub, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The estimate scales the engine results of earlier rounds (P5 about -3.4k and P2 about +0.6k per $/MWh-day, P1 and P4 about -1.6M at -40% WEST). It is an extrapolation.

A 30-day hot summer with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) and a deliberately small spread shock, so the scenario stays close to history on the congestion axis. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is only $35/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 35). The WEST on-peak price is a further 55% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -55) because upstate energy is bottled and demand is weak there, and real-time clears 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct -30) as day-ahead over-procures. Together these cut the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 well below the unshocked path. P5 loses on the spread. P2 and the small P3 gain partly offset these losses. Gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is rough because the price effects are not additive, so confidence is low.

A 22-day summer heat period with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Transfers into N.Y.C. are limited, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $75/MWh wider on each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75, inside the 289.7 historical maximum). That is the main loss, on P5, the N.Y.C. retail obligation short N.Y.C. with only a WEST hedge, and P2 returns about 18% of it. The WEST on-peak price is a further 20% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -20) because part of the upstate surplus cannot flow south, which removes some gains on the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Henry Hub, gas basis, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The estimate scales the spread results seen in earlier rounds (P5 about -3.4k and P2 about +0.6k per $/MWh-day) and adds a price effect of roughly -0.6M on P1 and P4. It is an extrapolation.

TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: gas_supply
Season: winter


INPUTS

{
 "active_positions": [
  "P1",
  "P2",
  "P3",
  "P4",
  "P5",
  "P6"
 ],
 "allocated_capital_usd": 20000000.0,
 "book": [
  {
   "channel": "system",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price is above K1",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",
   "position": "P1",
   "what": "Long 100 MW swap on the WEST on-peak price, strike K1 = 39.49 $/MWh, 16 h per on-peak weekday"
  },
  {
   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long winter pipeline constraint into the New York City area leaves Zone J gas-fired units short of fuel at the margin. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $70/MWh for all 30 days (spread shock). Henry Hub rises only 10% because the problem is local delivery, not national supply. Daily peak load runs 5% above a typical winter day (load ratio 1.05), which enlarges the Zone J retail obligation. P5 is short Zone J against a WEST hedge, so it loses heavily; from the winter sensitivities this is about $3.9k per $1/MWh per day net of the P2 gain. The small gas rise lifts WEST power slightly and gives P1 a small gain. The $15/MMBtu NY gas basis hits only the P4 heat-rate call. I estimate a net loss of roughly $8M, but the extrapolation from a 5-day sensitivity to 30 days is uncertain.

A two-week cold spell with a regional gas supply squeeze, similar in kind to the January 2025 cold event, when Z6 NY gas traded near $97.9/MMBtu against a Henry Hub of about $10.0. Henry Hub rises 40% and the NY gas basis adds $25/MMBtu, which lowers the P4 heat-rate payoff. Peak load runs 10% above a typical winter day, which scales up the Zone J obligation. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $120/MWh for 15 days. That is within the historical range and well below the Elliott RT spread, and it is the main loss driver through P5. The P1 gain from higher gas, about $0.4M over the period, only partly offsets the spread loss. My estimate is a net loss of about $7M. The estimate rests on scaling the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A month in which gas costs rise while WEST power does not follow. Henry Hub is up 50% and the NY gas basis adds $20/MMBtu. Surplus upstate hydro, wind and imports push WEST on-peak 45% below what gas and load imply, so the heat rate compresses. P1 and P4, both long WEST power, lose, and P4 also suffers from the basis. Constrained downstate gas supply widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $55/MWh for all 30 days, which hurts P5 more than it helps P2. Load is held at the normal level. The spread loss is about $6.4M, P1 is roughly -$0.4M net of the gas effect, and P4 adds a small further loss. The total is about -$6.5M, but the WEST power move is not internally verified and the confidence is low.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

I scaled the 5-day winter sensitivities to 30 days. P5 loses roughly $7.0M, P2 gains about $0.9M, P1 gains about $0.8M and P4 loses about $0.5M. The net loss is about $5.8M, which is an uncertain extrapolation.

A month in which gas supply problems hit downstate while upstate power stays soft. Henry Hub is up 15% and the NY gas basis adds $12/MMBtu. Strong upstate hydro, wind and imports hold the WEST on-peak price 25% below what gas and load imply, so the heat rate compresses. This hurts the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and it reduces the WEST hedge leg of P5. Constrained downstate fuel widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $50/MWh for all 30 days, and this hurts P5 more than it helps P2. Load is only 3% above normal, so the loss comes mainly from the spread and the weak WEST price. My estimate is P5 about -$5.7M, P2 +$0.9M, P1 about -$0.4M net of the gas effect and P4 about -$0.5M. The net loss is about $5.7M, and the WEST price move is not verified against history.

A three-week gas delivery failure into the New York City area, shorter but more intense than a month-long squeeze. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $90/MWh for 20 days (spread shock), which drives the loss through P5, the short Zone J retail obligation. Henry Hub rises 30% and the NY gas basis adds $10/MMBtu, which only lowers P4. Peak load runs 6% above a typical winter day, which scales up the P5 obligation. There is no extra WEST power shock, so the P1 gain from gas and load partly offsets the loss. I scaled the 5-day sensitivities to 20 days. P5 loses about $7.0M, P2 gains about $1.1M, P1 gains about $0.6M and P4 loses about $0.4M. The net loss is about $5.8M, which is an uncertain extrapolation.

1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).

scenario.narrative: Large loads (data centers) arrive about 900 MW slower than forecast, and the daily peak runs about 5% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). The softer upstate load leaves WEST prices weak while N.Y.C. stays tight, because transfers into the load pocket stay limited. This is a congestion and zone-volume channel, so pocket_minus_ref_usd is +110 $/MWh for 20 days. That is well inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. The retail obligation P5 (short 140 MW in N.Y.C., hedged in WEST) loses roughly $4,200 per day for each $1 of widening. The long spread P2 recovers only about $770 per day for each $1. Net, the book loses about $3,400 per day per $1, or roughly $7.5M over 20 days. The lower load costs P1 and P4 a further small amount. Gas, WEST on-peak extra move, real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are left at zero. Estimate is scaled from the 5-day sensitivities assuming linearity, so uncertainty is material.

Large loads fall 1500 MW short of forecast, in line with the Gold Book typical day-ahead load forecast miss of -1500 MW. The daily peak is about 10% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.90). A long, soft period follows. WEST on-peak price drops a further 60% (ref_onpeak_pct -60) on top of the load effect, which hits the long 100 MW swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Henry Hub gas falls 40% (gas_hh_pct -40) with weak burn, which lowers power prices further. Real-time clears 50% below day-ahead (dart_pct -50) because day-ahead over-forecasts load; this also reduces P1 and P4 through the price path. The spread widens modestly by 40 $/MWh as WEST softens faster than N.Y.C., which hurts P5. The shocks last 30 days. The main loss is the system channel (P1/P4), with the P5 spread loss second, and no spike days. Estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities and the effects are not additive, so uncertainty is material.

N.Y.C. stays constrained while WEST weakens. The spread widens by 60 $/MWh for 30 days, which is the main loss through the retail load obligation P5, only partly offset by the long spread P2. Gas falls 30% (gas_hh_pct -30) on weaker demand. WEST on-peak falls a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35), which cuts the long swap P1 and heat-rate call P4. Real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are left at zero, so the P3 and P6 channels are quiet. The mix is congestion-led with a moderate system and gas component. The estimate is scaled linearly from 5-day sensitivities and discounted for non-additivity.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 300 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -300), and the daily peak runs 3% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.97). Upstate softens while N.Y.C. stays import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 65 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 65) for the full 30 days. That is inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. This hurts the retail load obligation P5, which loses about $3,300 per day for each $1 of widening, only partly offset by the long spread P2 at about $600 per day per $1. WEST on-peak falls a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15) and Henry Hub falls 10% (gas_hh_pct -10) on weaker demand, which costs the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 a smaller amount. Real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are zero. The estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities and the effects are not additive, so uncertainty is material.

Large loads fall about 1,400 MW short of forecast (large_load_shock_mw -1400, matching the shortfall_2035_mw figure in the Gold Book series). The daily peak runs 10% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.90). A soft 30-day period follows, and this scenario is led by the system channel. WEST on-peak falls a further 75% (ref_onpeak_pct -75) on top of the load effect, which hits the long 100 MW swap P1. Henry Hub falls 35% (gas_hh_pct -35) on weak gas burn, which cuts P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Real-time clears 20% below day-ahead (dart_pct -20) because day-ahead over-forecasts load, which also lowers P1. The spread widens only 25 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 25), so P5 is the second loss source and P2 recovers part of it. There are no spike days. The estimate is scaled from 5-day sensitivities with a discount for non-additivity, so uncertainty is material.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 600 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -600), and the daily peak is 5% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Upstate is oversupplied while N.Y.C. stays tight behind its transfer limits. The spread widens by 85 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 85) for 25 days, a shorter but wider congestion episode than the earlier ones, and below the summer historical maximum of 289.7. The retail load obligation P5 takes most of the loss, about $3,250 per day for each $1 of widening, and the long spread P2 offsets about $600 per day per $1. The lower load also trims P1 and P4 slightly. Gas, the extra WEST on-peak move, real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are all zero, so this is a pure zone-volume and congestion scenario. The estimate is scaled linearly from 5-day sensitivities, so uncertainty is material.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 800 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -800) and the daily peak is 5% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.95). The softer upstate market pushes WEST on-peak down a further 50% (ref_onpeak_pct -50), which cuts the long 100 MW swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Henry Hub falls 20% (gas_hh_pct -20) on weak gas burn, a small extra drag on P4. N.Y.C. stays constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 50 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50) over 28 days. That hurts the retail obligation P5 at roughly $3,300 per day per $1, only partly offset by the long spread P2 at $600 per day per $1. Real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are zero. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results, and the effects are not additive, so uncertainty is material.

Large loads arrive only about 150 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -150) and the daily peak is 1% below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.99), so load stays near normal and P5 keeps its full size. N.Y.C. stays tight behind its transfer limits while WEST is oversupplied, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 80 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80) for the full 30 days. That is far inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. This is the main loss, through the retail load obligation P5, and P2 only offsets about $600 per day per $1. A New York gas basis of +5 $/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 5) raises the gas cost seen by the heat-rate call P4 only, so P4 loses part of its payoff without moving power prices. All other shocks are zero. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results, so uncertainty is material.

A short, sharp episode lasting 15 days. Large loads arrive about 1,000 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -1000) and the daily peak is 6% below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.94). WEST on-peak falls a further 50% (ref_onpeak_pct -50) as upstate supply overwhelms demand, which hits the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Henry Hub falls 15% (gas_hh_pct -15), a small extra drag on P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 120 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 120), well inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. P5 takes the main loss at roughly $3,300 per day per $1, with P2 offsetting about $600 per day per $1. Real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are zero. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results, and the effects are not additive, so uncertainty is material.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads arrive about 200 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -200), but the daily peak stays at a typical summer level (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so P5 keeps its full size. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 45 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45) for 30 days because N.Y.C. stays import-constrained while upstate is long. Earlier results put the P5 loss at about $3,300 per day per $1 of widening, with the long spread P2 recovering about $600. WEST on-peak falls a further 60% (ref_onpeak_pct -60) and Henry Hub falls 20% (gas_hh_pct -20), which cut the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. Real-time clears 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct -30), which adds a small further drag on P1. There are no spike days. This is a smaller-spread, system-assisted mix. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results and the effects are not additive, so uncertainty is material.

Large loads arrive about 400 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -400) and the daily peak is 2% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.98). Weak upstate demand leaves WEST soft while N.Y.C. stays tight, so the spread widens by 55 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55) for 30 days. This hits the retail obligation P5 at about $3,300 per day per $1, partly offset by the long spread P2. WEST on-peak falls a further 40% (ref_onpeak_pct -40), which cuts the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A New York gas basis of +6 $/MMBtu (ny_gas_basis_usd 6) raises the gas cost seen only by P4, so its payoff falls without moving power prices. Henry Hub, real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are zero. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results, and uncertainty is material.

Large loads arrive about 700 MW slower than forecast (large_load_shock_mw -700) and the daily peak is 4% below a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 0.96). A 22-day episode follows in which N.Y.C. stays constrained behind its transfer limits while upstate is oversupplied, so the spread widens by 95 $/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 95), still well inside the summer historical maximum of 289.7. P5 takes the main loss at about $3,300 per day per $1, with P2 offsetting about $600. WEST on-peak falls a further 30% (ref_onpeak_pct -30) and Henry Hub falls 10% (gas_hh_pct -10) on weaker burn, which costs P1 and P4 a smaller amount. Real-time vs day-ahead and spikes are zero. This is a medium-length, wide-spread congestion episode. The estimate is scaled from earlier engine results, and uncertainty is material.
